prize_parts.citation: For the development of ionizable lipid nanoparticles for the delivery of nucleic-acid medicines

statement.case_for: Ionizable lipid nanoparticles are a molecular design achievement: pH-dependent charge and lipid polymorphism were engineered so that one particle encapsulates nucleic acid at manufacture, stays inert in blood and opens the endosome on demand. That design logic, together with rapid-mixing formation, made siRNA drugs and mRNA vaccines possible and gave medicine a general delivery platform, which is exactly the test I apply of whether researchers and clinicians can now do something they could not do before. The evidence is mature and independent (an approved siRNA drug, billions of vaccine doses, many replicating groups), so there is no maturity risk.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that this is pharmaceutical formulation rather than chemistry, and that the 2023 Medicine prize already covers the mRNA vaccine story, so the committee could see it as a second reward for the same outcome. Attribution is also genuinely hard: six credited names compete for three places, and my opening trio (Cullis, Anderson, MacLachlan) leaves out people with early claims.

responses.point: Sparr ranks B062 first as lipid self-assembly put to work, with Cullis, Madden and Hope as the early formulation core.
responses.response: I agree with her chemistry framing, and it is the best answer to the 'not chemistry' objection: bilayer versus non-bilayer phase behaviour and pKa-tuned charge are physical chemistry. Her argument for Madden and Hope as originators of encapsulation persuades me to move from my opening trio (Cullis, Anderson, MacLachlan) to Cullis, Madden and Hope. My remaining worry is that this trio omits the later ionizable-lipid optimisation and clinical siRNA translation, which is where Anderson and MacLachlan matter. I am relying on memory of that history, not on the files.

responses.point: Linke, as chair, ranks PROTACs and molecular glues (B027) first as a clear mechanistic principle and a new modality, and notes the glue branch would crowd a three-person citation.
responses.response: I take the mechanistic clarity seriously, and I ranked B027 second myself. But I would qualify the case: no degrader is approved, so the impact on what clinicians can do is still prospective, whereas LNPs have already delivered. The Crews/Deshaies versus Handa split also looks like two discoveries under one heading, which a three-person cap handles badly. I would hold B027 for a later year rather than award it now over B062.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks Car-Parrinello ab initio molecular dynamics first as a clean, mature, arguably overdue two-laureate case.
responses.response: The attribution is indeed cleaner than mine and the maturity beyond doubt, which counts for a lot. My disagreement is about breadth of consequence for experimentalists and clinicians: the method is powerful for computation but its reach outside theory is indirect. If the committee prizes clean attribution and maturity above downstream change, B049 is a legitimate rival to B062, and I would not oppose it strongly. I am only one vote, and B049 has little support beyond him.

responses.point: Chabes ranks DNA base editing (B038) first as biology reduced to a defined deaminase reaction, preferring Liu alone.
responses.response: I share his appreciation for mechanism-to-tool stories and agree a Liu-only prize is the cleanest attribution on the list. I would qualify it with timing: the 2020 CRISPR prize and the still-short clinical record make base editing feel early, while LNP delivery is already proven in patients and is what lets base editors be delivered in vivo, so I rank it below B062.

uncertainties: How to divide credit among Cullis, Hope, Madden, MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer, since my account of the lipid-development history is from memory and unverified.
Whether the committee accepts LNP delivery as chemistry given the 2023 Medicine prize on mRNA modification.
Whether PROTACs and glues will have enough clinical proof, or an agreed credit split, to overtake LNPs this year.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My profile lists no tie to the LNP, PROTAC or other shortlisted candidates, only a general overlap in peptide and self-assembly research with Emma Sparr, which does not require recusal.
